At the heart of AgentFS is the agent filesystem, a complete SQLite-based storage system for agents implemented using Turso. Everything an agent does—every file it creates, every piece of state it stores, every tool it invokes—lives in a single SQLite database file.

Bubblewrap provides filesystem isolation using Linux namespaces and overlays. While you could achieve similar isolation with a `bwrap` call that mounts `/` read-only and uses `--tmp-overlay` on the working directory, the key difference is persistence and queryability: with AgentFS, the upper filesystem is stored in a single SQLite database file, which you can query, snapshot, and move to another machine. Read more about the motivation in the announcement blog post.

Docker Sandbox and AgentFS are complementary rather than competing. AgentFS answers "what happened and what's the state?" while Docker Sandboxes answer "how do I run this safely?" You could use both together: run an agent inside a Docker Sandbox for security, while using AgentFS inside that sandbox for structured state management and audit trails.

Git worktrees let you check out multiple branches of a repository into separate directories, allowing agents to work on independent copies of the source code—similar to AgentFS. But AgentFS solves the problem at a lower level. With git worktrees, nothing prevents an agent from modifying files outside its worktree: another agent's worktree, system files, or anything else on the filesystem. The isolation is purely conventional, not enforced. AgentFS provides filesystem-level copy-on-write isolation that's system-wide and cannot be bypassed—letting you safely run untrusted agents. And because it operates below git, it also handles untracked files, making it useful beyond just version-controlled source code.

`csv2sql` is a small simple program specifically designed to quickly convert a comma separated value (CSV) file into simple structured query language (SQL) statements, which can then be used as an import source for a SQLite database.

A few different approaches were tried over time (using tcl, Python), and c)) none of which were bad at the job—however the application was ported over to Go) (golang)—and it immediately benefited as Go has a great built-in CSV file handling (as well as other formats), and the speed to process the file was impressive too. It might not be as fast as c, or it might not be as simple to understand as tcl or Pyhton code wise at first, but overall it suited my requirements best. Go also supports UTF8 characters without extra work, and was cross platform too!

This command line parameter is required to allow the program to run properly, so is mandatory for successful use. Adapters that embed stratum inside a larger storage substrate (e.g. as a Datalog secondary index) can implement the `IAuditable` protocol on their wrapper types to compose stratum verification with other engines' verification in one pass. The result-map shape (`:ok`, `:mismatch`, `:unsupported`, `:advisory`, `:incomplete`) is stable so multi-engine drivers don't need translation layers. See doc/audit.md for the full surface.

Allen interval predicates (`OVERLAPS`, `CONTAINS`, `PRECEDES`, `MEETS`, …) and `FOR PORTION OF VALID_TIME` DML are supported; `FOR SYSTEM_TIME` DML is intentionally not exposed (audit-integrity by construction). See doc/temporal-design.md for the full design, including the rationale for the system-axis read-only stance and how stratum compares to XTDB / SQL:2011 RDBMSes / cloud-warehouse Time Travel.

**Bitemporal (SQL:2011)**: `FOR PORTION OF VALID_TIME` DML on bitemporal tables, `FOR VALID_TIME AS OF` / `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF` time-travel reads, Allen interval predicates (OVERLAPS / CONTAINS / PRECEDES / MEETS / …). See doc/temporal-design.md.

The DSL is intentionally flat. Every clause resolves column names by keyword lookup against a single merged map: `:from` establishes the base columns, `:join` merges in the dimension table's columns, and all subsequent clauses (`:where`, `:agg`, `:group`, `:select`, `:having`, `:order`) reference any column by its keyword. This makes it straightforward to build queries from Clojure data - no quoting, no SQL string interpolation, just maps and vectors. Composition (the DSL equivalent of SQL CTEs/subqueries) is done with Clojure `let`/`def` - see Column Scoping and Composition for details.
Stratum is part of the Replikativ ecosystem - a set of composable, immutable data systems:
- **Datahike** - immutable graph database with Datalog queries

- **Audit**: content-addressed `:crypto-hash?` commits, `stratum.audit/verify-chain` for tamper detection (shallow + deep PSS-tree walks), `IAuditable` protocol for embedding into larger storage substrates (doc/audit.md)
- **Bitemporal**: SQL:2011 valid- and system-time axes, `FOR PORTION OF VALID_TIME` DML, `FOR (VALID|SYSTEM)_TIME AS OF` time-travel reads, Allen interval predicates (doc/temporal-design.md)

|**No joined rows**|Computes the result as the matrix product XᵀX, where X has one row per key and one column per value, in one pass over the input.|
|**Sparse first**|Computes each pair of values once in a dense array of counters and writes only the nonzero cells. Results larger than the memory limit go to disk.|

|**Pruning**|With `HAVING` or `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`, drops the values that cannot reach the threshold before any product, so stricter queries run faster. Results stay exact. DuckDB, PostgreSQL, and Spark pass both forms, and SQLite its `min` argument.|
|**Dense core on AMX**|Runs the small dense block of the most frequent values as 8-bit tiles on the CPU matrix accelerator.|
|**Exact integer sums**|Sums integer weights exactly, in 64 or 128 bits, and raises the engine's own overflow error wherever the engine's plan would.|

|**Cost-based frontier**|The two paths meet at the dense frontier, which a cost model places for each query where an accelerator tile costs as much as the sparse products it replaces. Pruning runs first, so the frontier follows the query, and it stays empty when no block pays off.|

|**Inside the engine**|Hooks into the planners of DuckDB, PostgreSQL, and Spark, so the SQL runs unchanged, and into SQLite as table functions. Follows each engine's cancellation, thread count, and errors, keeps the output within the memory limit of DuckDB, PostgreSQL, and SQLite, and spills the rest to the engine's temporary space within its limit.|

|`tessera_c_set_many_int`, `tessera_c_add_many2`, `tessera_c_next_many2`, `tessera_c_many_overflow`|Exact integer sums among them, each sum's overflow, and NULL factors: a pair adds to a sum only when neither row marks it NULL, and a sum without such a pair comes back NULL|

|`tessera_c_set_group_top`|The top values of each group: only the cells that can reach rank `k` of their group come back. The group is column 0 when both orders of a pair are rows (`0`), the column holding the lower or higher key (`1`, `2`), or the cross product's x or y (`3`, `4`)|

|`tessera_c_set_float_errors`, `tessera_c_set_float_accum`, `tessera_c_float_errors`|Whether a product of two doubles overflowed or underflowed to zero, for an engine that raises an error then. `tessera_c_set_float_accum` adds the overflow of an `AVG`'s running sum (PostgreSQL's `float8_accum`), and a row value `TESSERA_C_ROW_VALUE_OVERFLOW` or `TESSERA_C_ROW_VALUE_UNDERFLOW` marks a row whose own factors did so|
|`tessera_c_set_sum_limit`|The magnitude above which an integer sum is an error or NULL in the engine: no pruning unless every sum stays below it|
|`tessera_c_general`|Whether the values come back as doubles (`vd`) rather than integers (`vi`)|

apitame: tame any API or database for AI agents. One command turns an OpenAPI or Swagger spec or a PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite database into a safe MCP server plus an agent skill (SKILL.md) for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code and Gemini CLI. Stripe
Turn any OpenAPI spec or SQL database into a safe MCP server, plus agent skills. One command.
Terminal demo: apitame init turns a 38-endpoint GitHub API spec into 8 read-only tools, inspect shows about 60% fewer tokens, test passes and add-to installs it in Claude Code
The connection string is saved to `.env` (never to the config file). Use a read-only role: docs/sql.md has a two-line setup.

DuckDB's driver is an optional extra (its native binary adds 40 to 120 MB), so it is not part of the default install: run apitame with `npx -p apitame -p @duckdb/node-api@1.5.6-r.1 apitame <command>` (the tested release), and `add-to` writes client configs that do the same. DuckDB runs in a separate process with memory, thread and time limits. See DuckDB.

Prefer HTTP? `npx apitame serve --transport http` listens on `http://127.0.0.1:3333/mcp` (destructive actions are approved in the client: right away for clients on MCP protocol 2026-07-28, with `--sessions` for older clients). To share it with a team, `http.oauth` lets your identity provider sign each user in and apitame check their access tokens, and `http.oauth.permissions` gives each scope or client its own tools and writes. More in docs/clients.md. The container image (`ghcr.io/albert-canfield/apitame`) and docs/deploy.md cover running it behind a reverse proxy with TLS.
|Read-only mode (default)|Write operations are not exposed as tools, and `call_operation` refuses them. Anything other than GET, HEAD and OPTIONS counts as a write unless you mark it as a read.|
|Allowlist|In `read-write` mode, only operations in `writes.allow` run. Wildcards like `create*` work.|
|Confirmation|DELETE and anything named like delete, remove, purge, cancel or bulk is destructive and always needs approval, through MCP elicitation or a one-time token bound to the exact arguments.|
|Dry run|`"dryRun": true` on any write returns the exact request (or, for SQL, the affected row count in a rolled-back transaction) without changing anything.|
|Validation|Arguments are checked against the operation's schema before anything is sent. Unknown parameters are rejected.|
|Limits|Per-request timeout and response size cap. Large JSON is trimmed to fit, with a note saying how much was kept.|

|Secrets|Credentials come only from environment variables or a secret manager, read through its CLI at startup (inline secrets in the config are refused), and are redacted from results, errors, logs and previews, even when an API echoes them back.|
|HTTP transport|Loopback only by default, with Host and Origin checks. Listening on another interface requires a bearer token, or OAuth access tokens from your identity provider.|
|Outgoing requests|Path parameters cannot be `.` or `..`; credentials never follow a redirect to another host; files are passed inline, never as local paths, and uploads are capped.|
|Rate limits|By default 120 calls and 20 writes per minute, so a looping agent cannot hammer an API or database. With OAuth, each user can also get a budget of their own.|
|Audit log|Optional JSON Lines record of every write attempt (blocked, dry run, confirmed, sent) and every refused query, with secrets redacted.|
Read docs/safety.md for the full model, including what apitame does not protect against.
|`apitame init `|Introspect an OpenAPI or Swagger file or URL, a `postgres://` or `mysql://` URL, or a SQLite or DuckDB file. Writes `apitame.config.yaml` and `skills/`.|
|`apitame serve`|Run the MCP server over stdio (default) or `--transport http`. With `--watch`, config and spec edits apply live and clients are told the tools changed.|
|`apitame inspect`|List tools, access levels and estimated token cost. `--max-tokens <n>` fails CI when the tool list grows past a budget.|

|`apitame diff <old-spec> [new-spec]`|Show what a new version of the spec changes for the agent: operations added, removed or renamed, access level changes, new writes that a wildcard in `writes.allow` would let through, config entries left behind and token cost. `--fail-on new-writes` blocks a pull request in CI. Never calls the API.|

|`apitame test`|Call every read tool against a local mock built from the spec (or `--live`, which also validates responses), and prove that blocked writes are refused. For SQL, check every table and try known injection payloads.|
|`apitame add-to <client>`|Print or `--write` the config for `claude-code`, `codex`, `cursor`, `vscode`, `gemini` or `claude-desktop`, and install the skills.|

|`apitame doctor`|Check the setup end to end: config, environment variables, secret manager references, `.env` safety, API or database connectivity and credentials, whether the database role could write, skills and client configs, and for HTTP deployments authentication, the OAuth issuer and keys and the public URL behind the proxy (`--host 0.0.0.0`).|
